title: Classical Christian Dictionary #5
author: Doug Wilson
summary: In the fifth installment of his running Classical Christian Dictionary series, Doug Wilson defines seven terms central to the classical Christian education movement's vocabulary and history, ranging from apologist figures (Chesterton, C.S. Lewis) to reading-instruction methods (look-say versus phonics) to foundational pedagogical texts (Dorothy Sayers's "Lost Tools of Learning," John Milton Gregory's Seven Laws of Teaching) and institutions (the Society for Classical Learning). Wilson uses each entry to make a small argument as much as to define a term: the look-say method reduced words to memorized "squiggles" like Chinese characters and needlessly limited vocabulary, while phonics has "worked well for centuries" despite English's irregularities. He is careful to correct a common misreading of Dorothy Sayers, insisting her Trivium-based "stages" framework was a deliberate modern adaptation for universal education, not a literal return to how medieval children were actually taught, crediting Comenius for the underlying insight about sequenced prerequisites that made mass education possible. The entries on Lewis and Chesterton double as brief case studies in how classical formation shapes a mind, with Lewis's biography offered as "a standing illustration of what a rigorous classical education can do with someone with his native talent."
points: Wilson's Look Say entry makes a specific pedagogical argument, not just a definition: the whole-word method reduced sound-decodable words to memorized visual 'squiggles' comparable to Chinese characters, which necessarily limited vocabulary and left unusual words permanently inaccessible to students.

The Sayers Insight entry corrects a common misconception in the classical education movement itself, insisting Dorothy Sayers's Trivium-stages framework was a deliberate modern adaptation for universal education, crediting Comenius specifically for the underlying sequenced-prerequisite insight, rather than a literal restoration of medieval pedagogy.

John Milton Gregory's Seven Laws of Teaching are reproduced in full sequence, giving the entry the weight of a primary-source teaching document rather than a mere historical footnote, and situating it explicitly as foundational to 'the classical Christian education movement.'

The SCL and ACCS entry positions two of the movement's major institutional bodies against each other along a specific axis (broader/more liberal outlook versus its 'older sister'), giving readers a concrete map of the movement's internal institutional landscape rather than treating it as monolithic.

It is important to emphasize that this was an adaptation, and not an attempt to return the way younger children were actually taught in the Middle Ages.

When Dorothy Sayers applied the three aspects of the Trivium to the three stages of child development, she was responsible for the Sayers Insight. This was to combine the categories of the Trivium with the need for a structured and graded education, with prerequisites.
They have a broader and more liberal outlook than does her older sister, ACCS, but at the same time the two organizations continue to have an overlapping constituency.
